title: Secure defaults and least privilege

thumbnail.alt: Video thumbnail for Secure defaults and least privilege

children.text: Most breaches exploit something that was left open rather than something clever. Default deny, then grant the narrow thing that is needed.
What this lesson covers
Default to deny and grant explicitly
Scope credentials to the minimum they need
Reduce attack surface by removing unused paths
This lesson sits in Thinking About Threats, part of Practical Web Security. It assumes what came before it and leads directly into the next lesson in the module.

keyPoints: Default to deny and grant explicitly
Scope credentials to the minimum they need
Reduce attack surface by removing unused paths

title: Cross-site scripting (XSS)

children.text: XSS is attacker-controlled content executing as script in your page. Contextual output encoding is the fix; blocklists are not.
What this lesson covers
Tell stored, reflected, and DOM-based XSS apart
Encode output for the context it lands in
Constrain script sources with a content security policy
This lesson sits in Common Web Vulnerabilities, part of Practical Web Security. It assumes what came before it and leads directly into the next lesson in the module.

keyPoints: Tell stored, reflected, and DOM-based XSS apart
Encode output for the context it lands in
Constrain script sources with a content security policy

title: SQL injection

children.text: Injection happens when data becomes part of the query. Parameterised queries keep the two separate, and they are not optional.
What this lesson covers
See how concatenated input changes a query
Use parameterised queries everywhere
Limit database privileges to contain the damage
This lesson sits in Common Web Vulnerabilities, part of Practical Web Security. It assumes what came before it and leads directly into the next lesson in the module.

keyPoints: See how concatenated input changes a query
Use parameterised queries everywhere
Limit database privileges to contain the damage
proTip: Never build a query with string concatenation. Parameters are the whole defence, not a style preference.

title: Cross-site request forgery

thumbnail.alt: Video thumbnail for Cross-site request forgery

children.text: CSRF makes a logged-in user’s browser send a request they never intended. SameSite cookies and anti-forgery tokens close it.

Validate anti-forgery tokens on state-changing requests

title: Sessions versus JWTs

thumbnail.alt: Video thumbnail for Sessions versus JWTs

children.text: Server sessions are revocable; JWTs are stateless and awkward to revoke. Pick based on whether you need to log someone out immediately.
What this lesson covers
Compare revocability and statelessness honestly
Store tokens in cookies with the right flags
Design refresh and logout before you ship
This lesson sits in Authentication Done Right, part of Practical Web Security. It assumes what came before it and leads directly into the next lesson in the module.

keyPoints: Compare revocability and statelessness honestly
Store tokens in cookies with the right flags
Design refresh and logout before you ship

title: Password storage and hashing

thumbnail.alt: Video thumbnail for Password storage and hashing

children.text: Passwords are hashed with a slow, salted algorithm designed for the job. Anything faster is a favour to whoever steals the table.
What this lesson covers
Use a slow, salted hash such as argon2 or bcrypt
Tune work factors as hardware improves
Handle reset flows without leaking account existence
This lesson sits in Authentication Done Right, part of Practical Web Security. It assumes what came before it and leads directly into the next lesson in the module.

keyPoints: Use a slow, salted hash such as argon2 or bcrypt
Tune work factors as hardware improves
Handle reset flows without leaking account existence
proTip: Never write your own password hashing. Use a vetted algorithm with sane parameters and move on.

title: MFA and delegated authentication

keyPoints: Add a second factor without wrecking usability
Distinguish OAuth authorization from OIDC identity

Introduce a content security policy incrementally

title: Secrets management

children.text: Secrets belong in a manager, injected at runtime, never in the repository. Assume anything committed once is compromised forever.
What this lesson covers
Keep credentials out of source control
Inject secrets at runtime and scope them tightly
Rotate credentials and revoke exposed ones immediately
This lesson sits in Hardening and Supply Chain, part of Practical Web Security. It assumes what came before it and leads directly into the next lesson in the module.

keyPoints: Keep credentials out of source control
Inject secrets at runtime and scope them tightly
Rotate credentials and revoke exposed ones immediately
proTip: A secret committed once is compromised even after you delete the commit. Rotate it, do not just remove it.

title: Dependency and supply chain risk

thumbnail.alt: Video thumbnail for Dependency and supply chain risk

children.text: Most of your production code came from someone else. Lockfiles, audits, and update discipline are what keep that manageable.

Review what a new dependency actually pulls in
